sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Sharding is the practice of splitting a large logical database into smaller **horizontal shards** distributed across multiple physical machines, where each shard owns a non-overlapping subset of rows chosen by a **shard key**, so that storage and query load scale horizontally past the limits of a single server.

Sharding is the answer to the question: "What happens when one database machine can no longer hold the data or absorb the write rate?" Vertical scaling (bigger box) hits a ceiling — you cannot buy a server with petabytes of fast SSD and terabytes of RAM at any price. Sharding solves this by partitioning rows across N machines: each shard stores roughly 1/N of the data and handles roughly 1/N of the queries, so the cluster capacity scales linearly with shard count. The trade-off is **operational complexity**: queries that span multiple shards become slow (scatter-gather), cross-shard transactions are expensive or impossible, resharding is painful, and the shard key choice locks in future scalability. Sharding is not a feature you turn on — it is an architectural commitment that touches application code, deployment topology, and failure modes.

The central design decision is the **shard key** — the column (or composite) whose value determines which shard stores a row. A good shard key has three properties: (1) **high cardinality** so data spreads evenly (user_id is good; country_code with 200 values is bad if one country dominates); (2) **monotonic writes avoidable** so a single shard doesn't become a hot write target (an auto-incrementing timestamp makes all new rows land on one shard — the "hot shard" problem); (3) **query locality** so most application queries hit a single shard (queries that filter by `WHERE user_id=?` are O(1) shard lookups if `user_id` is the key). Real-world: Instagram shards its user data by `user_id` — every photo, comment, like, and follow for a given user lives on the same shard, so a profile page is a single-shard read. The shard key was chosen because virtually every Instagram query is "show me content for user X," and `user_id` has both high cardinality (1B+ users) and even distribution (no single user owns most data).

The three main sharding strategies are **range-based**, **hash-based**, and **directory-based**. Range-based sharding assigns contiguous key ranges to shards (`shard 0: user_id 0-1M`, `shard 1: 1M-2M`, ...). Pros: range queries (`WHERE user_id BETWEEN 100 AND 200`) hit a single shard. Cons: hot shards if the key is monotonic (new users always land on the last shard). Hash-based sharding computes `hash(shard_key) % N` to pick a shard. Pros: even distribution even with monotonic keys. Cons: range queries scatter-gather across all shards. Directory-based sharding uses a lookup table mapping key → shard, allowing arbitrary placement. Pros: flexible rebalancing. Cons: the lookup table itself is a bottleneck and SPOF (typically solved with a replicated Redis cluster). The fourth, more sophisticated strategy is **consistent hashing** (used by Cassandra, Dynamo, Redis Cluster) — keys are placed on a ring of hash values, and each shard owns a contiguous arc. Adding or removing a shard only moves keys between the new neighbor and existing nodes (O(1/N) data movement) instead of remapping everything (O(N) data movement under `% N`). This is critical for resharding.

Resharding — adding or removing shards as traffic grows — is the hardest operational problem. With naive `hash(key) % N`, going from N=10 to N=11 shards remaps roughly 90% of keys to different shards (every key whose hash modulo 11 differs from modulo 10). Moving petabytes of data is infeasible. The standard solutions: (1) **Consistent hashing** — only the keys in the new shard's arc move, typically 1/N of total data. (2) **Double the cluster** — going from N to 2N shards only remaps 50% of keys under `% N`, and each old shard splits in half. This is why many systems grow by powers of two. (3) **Virtual nodes (vnodes)** — each physical shard hosts many virtual shards on the consistent-hash ring, smoothing data movement and load. Cassandra uses 256 vnodes per node by default. Real-world: Uber's trip data is sharded by `trip_id` with consistent hashing across a Cassandra cluster; when Uber expands to a new city or adds capacity, vnodes rebalance automatically with minimal operator intervention. The shard key `trip_id` (a UUID) ensures even distribution, and trips are immutable so resharding never needs to migrate "hot" in-flight data.

The failure modes of sharding are subtle. A **hot shard** emerges when the shard key has skew — e.g., if a celebrity joins Instagram, their shard handles 1000× the traffic of other shards. Mitigations: split the celebrity across sub-shards (Justin Bieber's data is on multiple shards), or move them to a dedicated "managed" shard. A **cross-shard transaction** (writing to two shards atomically) requires 2PC or Saga patterns — slow and complex. Most sharded systems forbid cross-shard transactions; application code must structure writes to fit one shard. A **scatter-gather query** (`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE created_at > ?`) hits every shard and merges — the latency is `max(shard_latencies)`, and a single slow shard dominates. Sharded systems often maintain pre-computed counts (denormalized) to avoid this. A **shard failure** takes down 1/N of users — sharded systems pair each shard with a synchronous replica (Topic 13) so failover is automatic.

SELECT COUNT(*) ..."] --> S0 Scatter --> S1 Scatter --> S2 Scatter --> S3 Scatter --> Merge["Merge + return"] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +------------------+ | Application | | (shard client) | +--------+---------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Shard Router / Proxy | | hash(shard_key) % N | +---+----+----+----+----+ | | | | +--------+ | | +--------+ v v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ |Shard0| |Shard1| |Shard2| |Shard3| |users | |users | |users | |users | |0-999 | |1k-2k | |2k-3k | |3k-4k | +--+---+ +--+---+ +--+---+ +--+---+ | | | | v v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ |Repl 0| |Repl 1| |Repl 2| |Repl 3| +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ Consistent hashing ring (resilient to add/remove): shard 0 / \ (arc A) (arc D) / \ shard 3 shard 1 \ / (arc C) (arc B) \ / shard 2 add shard 4 -> only arcs A,D shrink -> O(1/N) data moves ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The application issues a query scoped by the shard key (e.g., `user_id=42`). A shard-aware client (or proxy like Vitess, Citus) hashes the key and routes the request to the owning shard. Single-shard queries are O(1) network hops — same latency as an unsharded DB. 2. The shard's primary handles the write (or replica serves the read). Each shard is a self-contained database with its own replicas, backups, and failover. A shard failure affects only 1/N of users. 3. Scatter-gather queries (analytics, count, search) hit every shard in parallel, and the router merges results. Latency is bounded by the slowest shard; throughput is N× a single shard. Resharding with consistent hashing moves only O(1/N) of data when adding a shard.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Consistent hashing shard router demo.

Shows:
  1. A consistent-hash ring of shards
  2. Key -> shard placement via ring lookup
  3. Adding a shard: only ~1/N keys move (vs ~N/N under hash % N)
  4. Virtual nodes for even distribution

Run:  python3 sharding_demo.py
"""

import hashlib
import bisect
import random
from collections import defaultdict

class ConsistentHashRing:
    def __init__(self, vnode_count=128):
        self.vnode_count = vnode_count
        self.ring = []          # sorted list of (hash, node) -> we keep two lists
        self.hashes = []        # sorted hash values
        self.hash_to_node = {}  # hash -> node name

    def _hash(self, s: str) -> int:
        return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)

    def add_node(self, node: str):
        for i in range(self.vnode_count):
            h = self._hash(f"{node}#{i}")
            self.hash_to_node[h] = node
            bisect.insort(self.hashes, h)

    def remove_node(self, node: str):
        self.hashes = [h for h in self.hashes if self.hash_to_node.get(h) != node]
        self.hash_to_node = {h: n for h, n in self.hash_to_node.items() if n != node}

    def get_node(self, key: str) -> str:
        if not self.hashes:
            raise RuntimeError("empty ring")
        h = self._hash(key)
        idx = bisect.bisect_right(self.hashes, h)
        if idx == len(self.hashes):
            idx = 0
        return self.hash_to_node[self.hashes[idx]]

def measure_remap(keys, n_old, n_new, vnode_count=128):
    """How many keys remap when going from n_old to n_new shards?"""
    ring_old = ConsistentHashRing(vnode_count)
    for i in range(n_old):
        ring_old.add_node(f"shard-{i}")
    ring_new = ConsistentHashRing(vnode_count)
    for i in range(n_new):
        ring_new.add_node(f"shard-{i}")
    moved = sum(1 for k in keys if ring_old.get_node(k) != ring_new.get_node(k))
    return moved

def naive_modulo(keys, n):
    return {k: int(hashlib.md5(k.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % n for k in keys}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    random.seed(42)
    # 100k Instagram-style user_ids
    keys = [f"user:{i}" for i in range(100_000)]

    # Placement with 4 shards
    ring = ConsistentHashRing(vnode_count=128)
    for i in range(4):
        ring.add_node(f"shard-{i}")
    placement = defaultdict(list)
    for k in keys:
        placement[ring.get_node(k)].append(k)
    print("=== Consistent hashing, 4 shards ===")
    for shard, ks in sorted(placement.items()):
        print(f"  {shard}: {len(ks):,} users ({len(ks)/len(keys)*100:.1f}%)")

    # Resharding: 4 -> 5 shards
    moved_ch = measure_remap(keys, 4, 5)
    print(f"\n=== Reshard 4 -> 5 shards ===")
    print(f"  Consistent hashing: {moved_ch:,} keys moved "
          f"({moved_ch/len(keys)*100:.1f}%)  -- expected ~{100/5:.1f}%")

    # Naive hash % N comparison
    old_mod = naive_modulo(keys, 4)
    new_mod = naive_modulo(keys, 5)
    moved_mod = sum(1 for k in keys if old_mod[k] != new_mod[k])
    print(f"  Naive hash % N:     {moved_mod:,} keys moved "
          f"({moved_mod/len(keys)*100:.1f}%)  -- expected ~80%")

    # Hot shard simulation: 99% of traffic to one user
    print(f"\n=== Hot shard detection ===")
    hot_user = "user:42"
    print(f"  {hot_user} -> {ring.get_node(hot_user)}")
    print(f"  Mitigation: pin hot keys to dedicated 'managed' shard via directory override")
```

quiz.explanation: Sharding and partitioning both split data into smaller pieces, but they differ in scope. Partitioning divides a table within a single database into smaller physical units (partitions) that share the same engine, memory, and disk — it is a storage optimization that stays invisible to the deployment topology.

quiz.explanation: High cardinality: the key must have many distinct values so data spreads evenly. user_id (billions of values) is good; country_code (200 values, with skew toward the US and India) is bad — one shard will hold 80% of users. **Even write distribution: avoid keys where writes concentrate on one value.

two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator sends "prepare" to each shard, waits for all to ack, then sends "commit." If any shard fails to prepare, the coordinator aborts.
quiz.explanation: two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator sends "prepare" to each shard, waits for all to ack, then sends "commit." If any shard fails to prepare, the coordinator aborts. 2PC is slow (multiple round trips), blocking (shards hold locks during prepare), and fragile (if the coordinator crashes, shards block indefinitely — the "blocking problem").
